title: Meta Serverless
summary: A function-as-a-service platform at hyperscale: queue every invocation, run functions on shared warm worker pools, and use deferral and admission control to smooth spiky load across regions.

head: Type
Requirement
rows: Developers deploy functions; invoke via events, schedules or RPC
Trillions of invocations per day across many regions (Meta's XFaaS reports this scale)
High utilization: avoid idle reserved capacity
Protect downstream services from function-driven load spikes

blocks.text: Meta's XFaaS paper (SOSP 2023) describes running functions on shared worker pools where every worker can run any function, and deferring delay-tolerant calls. AWS Lambda's Firecracker microVMs are a contrast for isolation.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: Most invocations don't need an answer this second. If I can defer them to off-peak, the fleet can be sized near the average instead of the peak.

deploy(function_name, code_bundle, runtime, limits{memory, timeout, concurrency}, criticality)
invoke(function_name, args, mode: SYNC | ASYNC, deadline?, idempotency_key?)
schedule(function_name, cron)
status(invocation_id) -> QUEUED | RUNNING | SUCCEEDED | FAILED(retrying)

blocks.caption: Submit → durable queue → scheduler → shared warm workers

items: Submitter accepts the call, enforces quotas, writes to a durable queue, returns an invocation ID.
Schedulers pull by priority and deadline, check downstream rate limits, dispatch to a worker.
Workers are pre-warmed with many functions' code loaded (universal workers), so most calls skip cold start.
Results/retries are recorded; failures retry with backoff until deadline, then go to a dead-letter path.

sections.title: Deep dive: scheduling and load shifting

items: Classify by criticality and deadline: user-facing sync calls run now; async calls with hours of slack can wait.
**Time shifting:** defer delay-tolerant work to off-peak hours, flattening the daily curve.
**Space shifting:** route to regions with spare capacity (global dispatcher sees regional utilization).
Per-function concurrency limits and fair share so one tenant can't starve others.
Downstream protection: back off dispatch when a called service signals overload (adaptive rate limiting).

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: A queue in front of compute turns spiky demand into a schedulable backlog; deadlines tell you how much you're allowed to delay.

sections.title: Deep dive: cold starts and isolation

cols.title: Universal shared workers (XFaaS)
pros: Few cold starts: any worker runs any function
cons: Weaker isolation; trust model = internal code

items: Keep code bundles cached locally on workers; JIT warmup and snapshot/restore reduce startup.
Locality: send a function to workers that recently ran it.

head: Failure
Impact
Mitigation
rows: Per-function and per-downstream rate limits, circuit breakers
At-least-once retry; functions must be idempotent (idempotency key)
Exponential backoff + jitter, retry budget, DLQ

head: Decision

items.q: How do you guarantee a function runs exactly once?
items.a: You can't in general; deliver at-least-once and require idempotency keys stored by the function or platform.
On queue depth × age vs deadline, not CPU; keep headroom for sync traffic.

items.q: Sync calls through a queue — isn't that slow?
items.a: An in-memory fast path for sync, critical calls; durable queue for async.

items: Queue every invocation; deadlines define slack.
Universal warm workers kill most cold starts.
Protect downstreams with adaptive rate limits.
Scale on queue age, not CPU.
